chunks.title: About me
chunks.text: I am a Senior Technical Architect with 10 years of experience building scalable backend systems and AI-powered applications. I specialize in LLM-integrated architectures, RAG pipelines and microservices-based systems using Python, Laravel and cloud platforms. I deliver enterprise SaaS products with a strong focus on automation, scalability and reliability.

chunks.title: Case study: LLM and RAG document pipeline
chunks.text: I built a RAG-based document pipeline for very large legal-style cases, where a single case can contain 45,000+ pages. Standard chat interfaces could not ingest that volume and gave ungrounded answers, so the goal was to let users query and summarise the full case reliably.

chunks.title: RAG pipeline architecture
chunks.text: My pipeline goes OCR, then document parsing and chunking, then vector embeddings stored in PostgreSQL with pgvector, then retrieval, then an LLM (Claude or Gemini) through LangChain, and finally structured output such as case summaries, structured briefs and strategy notes. Ingestion runs as background jobs so there are no file size limitations.

chunks.title: RAG pipeline key decisions
chunks.text: Key decisions I made in the RAG pipeline: keep vectors in PostgreSQL with pgvector so documents, metadata and embeddings live in one transactional store; process ingestion asynchronously in batches; attach page and document metadata to every chunk so answers can cite their source; and keep the LLM provider swappable between Claude and Gemini.

chunks.title: Case study: reducing hallucinations
chunks.text: I reduced hallucinations in AI outputs by implementing structured prompt pipelines and controlled retrieval mechanisms, so answers are grounded in retrieved source text rather than the model's general knowledge.

chunks.title: How I limit hallucinations
chunks.text: To limit hallucinations I constrain retrieval with relevance thresholds and metadata filters, break prompts into structured steps with fixed output schemas, instruct the model to answer only from supplied context and to say when information is missing, require citations back to source chunks, and validate outputs before they reach the user.

chunks.title: Case study: microservices SaaS platform

Services expose REST APIs, sit behind AWS infrastructure (EC2, RDS, S3, CloudFront), use Redis caching for performance and response times, and ship through Jenkins CI/CD pipelines with Docker.

chunks.title: Redis caching strategy
chunks.text: I implemented Redis-based caching strategies to improve system performance and response times, caching expensive reads and computed results with explicit expiry and invalidating keys when the underlying data changes.

chunks.title: CI/CD and AWS deployment

It roams the screen, shows reminders and take-a-break nudges, and reacts to the system: it dozes when you are idle, worries when the battery is low and gets bored when the CPU is pegged. chunks.title: Why pgvector over a dedicated vector database
chunks.text: I chose pgvector over a dedicated vector database because the documents, metadata and embeddings can live in one PostgreSQL store, which keeps filtering, joins and transactions simple, avoids running and syncing another system, and fits comfortably at the scale of per-case document sets.

chunks.title: Redis caching strategy decision
chunks.text: For caching I prefer a cache-aside pattern in Redis with explicit TTLs and event-based invalidation over write-through caching, because it keeps the database as the source of truth, degrades gracefully if Redis is unavailable, and only caches data that is actually read.

chunks.title: Why Flask for AI services alongside Laravel
chunks.text: I run AI and document-processing services in Python (Flask) next to Laravel for core product features, rather than forcing everything into one stack, because Python has the strongest ecosystem for LLM, embedding and OCR work while Laravel is very productive for business logic, admin and auth.

chunks.title: Why an on-device model over a cloud API
chunks.text: For workforce activity classification I chose a layered pipeline that tries a deterministic app lookup first and only then runs a small Qwen 0.8B ONNX vision model in a dedicated worker thread, instead of sending screenshots to a cloud API. Most activity is resolved by the cheap lookup, the model runs locally with no per-call API cost, and the worker thread keeps the app responsive.

chunks.title: Why store-and-forward and an alert state machine
chunks.text: In my solar monitoring system I chose an async MQTT gateway with a store-and-forward ring buffer persisted to JSONL, so no data is lost during broker disconnections. Instead of plain threshold alerts, anomalies go through a 5-state machine (Normal, Detecting, Confirmed, Diagnosed, Recovering) with LLM root-cause diagnosis and a 30-minute cooldown that prevents alert storms.

chunks.title: How this chat works
chunks.text: This chat runs entirely in your browser with no LLM and no API cost. It ranks my own content with BM25 keyword retrieval, keeps only chunks above a relevance threshold, and answers with extracted sentences plus source links, so it cannot invent facts. If nothing relevant is found it says so.
